quote: No. That's why the panels are located on less than optimal, location.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers that his existing system underperforms because of shading — a live pain point on his CURRENT solar investment. This is a strong reason to add panels/battery and directly explains his inbound interest, but the rep never asks a follow-up (how much is it underperforming, has he noticed a bill gap) that would have deepened the qualification.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to pause on self-disclosed dissatisfaction with the current install — a quick 'how much has that cost you in savings?' turns a logistics note into an emotional anchor for the closer.

quote: Alright. Let me see if I could get a better look here.
stewart_read: Customer has an existing system with Astrum and wants to add panels/battery — this is the orphaned_flow scenario. The rep captures ownership status and installer name but never asks if the system is currently working or whether Ken has had any issues beyond shading, both of which the orphaned_flow protocol calls for and which would surface useful context for the closer.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged this unnecessary since Ken clearly wants an ADD-ON rather than a replacement, making 'is it working' less relevant — but the schema still lists it as a required orphaned-flow check.
coaching_implication: Reinforce the full orphaned_flow checklist (own vs lease, company, size, working condition) even when the customer's ask sounds like a straightforward add-on — competitive/condition context still helps the closer.

quote: Last time I checked, it was 849.
stewart_read: Customer clears the credit qualifier decisively and the rep acknowledges it cleanly and moves on — correct, no issue here, included as a clean qualifier pass.
coaching_implication: No coaching needed — this is a properly executed qualifier check.

quote: Great. And then I have down here that you're paying about 200 a month on that electric bill. Is that accurate?
stewart_read: Rep surfaces a pre-existing bill figure from records rather than asking fresh, and when the customer disputes it ("That sounds a little high") the rep just agrees ("A little high, I would say") without probing for a corrected number or flipping it into motivation.
coaching_implication: When customer disputes a pre-filled bill number, that's an opening to ask 'so what would you estimate it's closer to?' rather than just agreeing it's high and moving to kWh collection.

stewart_read: Customer's pushback on the bill figure is a soft skepticism moment. The rep could flip it ('even if it's a bit lower, that's still money going straight to the utility instead of building equity in your own system') but instead just concedes the point and pivots to logistics.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read is more supported here — there is no evidence the rep is deferring this for a later strategic moment; the call ends shortly after without revisiting the bill.
coaching_implication: Practice a one-line bill flip for use even when the customer disputes the anchor number, rather than only when they confirm it.

quote: Yeah. Just send me an email, and I'll send it to you.
stewart_read: Customer offers a channel-preference workaround (email) for bill collection, and the rep accepts it flatly ('Okay. Yeah. Let's do that.') without tying the kWh data back to what it unlocks — e.g., how many panels or battery size it will support. No curiosity hook was planted before the call ends.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the driving constraint, spending extra time here may have been the wrong moment — a strategic read is plausible since the customer is not in a position to engage deeply right now.
coaching_implication: Even a one-line tie-back ('once we see your usage, we'll know exactly how much of that bill we can offset') costs no extra time and keeps the customer anchored on outcome, not just logistics.

quote: Okay. Yeah. No problem. We can pick it up in a couple hours then. You have a wonderful rest of your day.
stewart_read: The call ends with no specific callback time, no appointment date/time, and no verbal handshake. This is the button_up section entirely skipped — the rep had a legitimate reason (customer driving) but did not convert it into a scheduled callback slot.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic patience is plausible — pushing a driving customer for a hard time could feel pushy — but the rep could still have proposed a specific window ('does 6 tonight work for a callback?') without being aggressive, so the soft exit is more reactive than deliberate.
coaching_implication: Even on a deferred call, anchor a specific callback window before hanging up: 'No problem — I'll call you back around 6 tonight once you're home, does that work?' This alone would move the outcome from an open callback to a locked one.
